_about: Drafted reasons for predictor failures, keyed stat|A|B (either order). DRAFTS from Claude's training knowledge, NOT verified against a source; the teacher reviews each before flipping reviewed:true in docs/data/exceptions.json. Regenerate with: node tools/build_exceptions.mjs
radius_pm|As|Se: The Cordero radii of As (119 pm) and Se (120 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's own uncertainty: by group 15-16 of period 4 the across-period contraction has flattened because the filled 3d shell shields the added nuclear charge poorly.
radius_pm|As|Br: As (119 pm) and Br (120 pm) are 1 pm apart, within the Cordero uncertainty: the period-4 p-block radii level off after the 3d shell fills, so the across-period shrink is essentially gone by bromine.
radius_pm|Te|I: Te (138 pm) and I (139 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's uncertainty: the across-period contraction has flattened by the end of period 5 as the 4d shell shields poorly and the bonds measured are to larger partners.
radius_pm|Tl|Pb: Tl (145 pm) and Pb (146 pm) are 1 pm apart: in the period-6 p-block the across-period shrink is cancelled by the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding, leaving the radii nearly flat.
radius_pm|Tl|Bi: Period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat (Tl 145, Pb 146, Bi 148 pm) because relativistic 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding offset the usual across-period decrease, and Bi's three 6p electrons sit in the slightly larger 6p3/2 level.
radius_pm|Tl|At: Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) is an estimate from very few structures, and the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat anyway, so the across-period shrink from Tl (145 pm) does not show in this dataset.
radius_pm|Pb|Bi: Pb (146 pm) and Bi (148 pm) are 2 pm apart in a period whose p-block radii barely change: the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding cancel the usual across-period decrease.
radius_pm|Pb|At: Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) rests on very few structures and comes out larger than lead's (146 pm); the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat, so a small data artifact is enough to flip the order.
radius_pm|Bi|At: Astatine's 150 pm Cordero value is an estimate from scarce structural data and exceeds bismuth's 148 pm; across the flat period-6 p-block that 2 pm difference is within the method's uncertainty.
radius_pm|Po|At: Polonium's Cordero radius (140 pm) comes from few structures and astatine's (150 pm) from fewer still; the 10 pm jump is a data artifact of a sparsely measured corner of the table, not a trend.
ie1_kjmol|Be|B: Boron's outermost electron is in 2p, higher in energy and better shielded than beryllium's paired 2s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
ie1_kjmol|N|O: Oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair up in an already occupied orbital, and that pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of nitrogen's three unpaired, half-filled 2p electrons.
ie1_kjmol|Mg|Al: Aluminum's outermost electron is in 3p, higher in energy and better shielded than magnesium's paired 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
ie1_kjmol|Al|Ca: Aluminum's single 3p electron is unusually easy to remove (the s-to-p drop), while calcium is removing one of a filled 4s pair, so the heavier element edges ahead.
ie1_kjmol|Al|Ga: Gallium's 4p electron sits outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so the extra nuclear charge pulls it slightly harder than expected and the usual drop down the group vanishes.
ie1_kjmol|Al|Tl: Thallium's 6p electron is held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so its ionization energy is higher than aluminum's.
ie1_kjmol|P|S: Sulfur's fourth 3p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of phosphorus's three unpaired, half-filled 3p electrons.
ie1_kjmol|Ca|Ga: Gallium's single 4p electron is higher in energy than calcium's paired 4s electrons, so even with eleven more protons gallium's first ionization energy comes out lower.
ie1_kjmol|Ga|Tl: Thallium's 6p electron feels a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, and relativistic effects contract the inner shells further, so it is held more tightly than gallium's 4p electron.
ie1_kjmol|As|Se: Selenium's fourth 4p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it slightly easier to remove than one of arsenic's three unpaired 4p electrons.
ie1_kjmol|In|Tl: The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's 6p electron poorly (the lanthanide contraction), so the nucleus holds it tighter than indium holds its 5p electron.
ie1_kjmol|Sn|Pb: Lead's 6p electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so lead's ionization energy edges above tin's.
ie1_kjmol|Pb|Bi: In period 6 the 6p level splits strongly by spin-orbit coupling; bismuth's third 6p electron goes into the higher 6p3/2 level and is easier to remove than one of lead's lower 6p1/2 pair.
en_pauling|Al|Ga: Gallium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so gallium pulls bonding electrons harder than aluminum (the d-block contraction).
en_pauling|Al|In: Indium's valence electrons sit outside a filled 4d shell that shields poorly, so its electronegativity stays above aluminum's instead of falling down the group.
en_pauling|Al|Tl: Thallium's valence electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so it is more electronegative than aluminum.
en_pauling|Si|Ge: Germanium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so germanium pulls bonding electrons slightly harder than silicon (the d-block contraction).
en_pauling|Si|Sn: Tin's valence electrons sit outside filled 3d and 4d shells that shield poorly, so its electronegativity stays just above silicon's instead of falling down the group.
en_pauling|In|Tl: The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's valence electrons poorly and relativistic contraction tightens its hold, so thallium is slightly more electronegative than indium.
en_pauling|I|Xe: Xenon's Pauling value (2.6) is derived from its few compounds with fluorine and oxygen, and a noble gas does not continue the across-period rise, so iodine comes out higher.
mass|Ar|K: Argon's dominant isotope is Ar-40 while potassium's is K-39, so argon averages heavier even with one fewer proton; Earth's Ar-40 is abundant because it is the decay product of K-40.
mass|Te|I: Tellurium's most abundant isotopes are the heavy Te-128 and Te-130, while iodine is a single isotope, I-127, so tellurium's average mass exceeds iodine's despite the lower atomic number.
